title: Work, Energy, and Power: The Currency of Physics

questions.question: The work done by a force is zero when:
options: The body moves at constant speed
questions.rationale: With θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so W = Fs cos 90° = 0 — as when carrying a bag while walking on level ground.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of work?
questions.rationale: Work is measured in joules, where 1 J = 1 N·m; the watt measures power and the newton measures force.

questions.question: If the speed of a moving body doubles, its kinetic energy:
questions.rationale: KE = ½mv², so at 2v the energy is ½m(2v)² = 4 × ½mv² — four times larger.

questions.question: Using the lesson's example, a ball dropped from 20 m hits the ground at about:
questions.rationale: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 20) = √392 ≈ 20 m/s, as all the PE converts to KE.

questions.question: At the lowest point of a pendulum's swing:
options: PE is maximum, KE is minimum
KE is maximum, PE is minimum
questions.rationale: The pendulum trades PE for KE each swing: at the ends of the arc PE peaks; at the lowest point KE peaks.

questions.question: The unit of power is the:
questions.rationale: Power P = W/t is work per unit time, so its unit is the watt, defined as 1 joule per second.

questions.question: One kilowatt-hour equals how many joules?
In the lesson's example, a 100 W bulb burning for 10 hours consumes:
questions.rationale: 100 W × 10 h = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh, which is exactly one 'unit' on a domestic electricity bill.

questions.question: The work–energy theorem states that:
options: Net work equals the total energy of a body
Net work equals the power developed
Net work equals the change in kinetic energy
Net work equals the change in momentum
questions.rationale: The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy — pushing adds KE, friction removes it.
